questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 6 week history of a hoarse voice and 5 kg weight loss. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years. He has no sore throat or reflux symptoms. His left vocal cord does not move on laryngoscopy. Chest X-ray shows a left apical mass.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hoarse voice?
questions.e: An apical lung tumour has invaded the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, paralysing the left vocal cord; reflux or nodules leave a cord that still moves.

steps.x: This asks for the cause of one symptom: think about what an apical tumour can invade.

clues: smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years
left vocal cord does not move
steps.x: Smoker + weight loss + apical mass = lung cancer. A **fixed vocal cord** means the nerve, not the larynx, is the problem.

elim: He has no reflux symptoms and reflux does not paralyse a vocal cord.
Candida inflames the mucosa but does not stop a cord moving or cause an apical mass.
Nodules come from voice overuse and the cord still moves.
Viral laryngitis settles within 2 to 3 weeks and does not cause cord paralysis or weight loss.

steps.x: **C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy.** Hoarseness with a lung mass = recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion (and a contraindication to surgery).

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 4 week history of leg weakness, swollen ankles and a rounded face. She has smoked for 40 years and lost 6 kg. Her BP is 168/98 mmHg. Chest X-ray shows a right perihilar mass. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A central mass with weeks-onset Cushingoid features and marked hypokalaemia is ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer; squamous cell gives hypercalcaemia instead.

steps.x: Very rapid Cushing's with **low potassium** and weight loss (not weight gain) = **ectopic ACTH**. A **central/perihilar** mass in a heavy smoker = SCLC.

elim: Adenocarcinoma is peripheral and has no paraneoplastic hormone link.
A pituitary adenoma develops over years and does not cause a perihilar mass and weight loss.
Large cell carcinoma has no paraneoplastic association.
Squamous cell secretes PTHrP (high calcium), not ACTH.

steps.x: **D. Small cell lung cancer.** SCLC paraneoplastics: SIADH, ectopic ACTH (hypokalaemia), Lambert-Eaton.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has a 3 month history of cough, weight loss and painful swollen wrists and ankles. He has a 60 pack-year smoking history. He has finger clubbing and tenderness over the distal radius and tibia. Chest X-ray (see item resources) shows a thick-walled cavitating mass in the right upper zone. Sputum AFB smears are negative.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Thick-walled cavitating mass in the right upper zone.

questions.q: Which type of lung cancer is most likely?
questions.e: Cavitation plus hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing with distal long bone pain) point to squamous cell carcinoma, the cavitating, central NSCLC.

steps.x: Clubbing with painful distal long bones = **hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy**. A **cavitating** mass with negative AFB smears = squamous cell.

elim: Adenocarcinoma is peripheral and does not typically cavitate.
Large cell is poorly differentiated with no classic cavitation or HPOA link.
Mesothelioma is a pleural tumour with effusion and pleural thickening, not a lung cavity.
SCLC is central and does not cavitate; its syndromes are hormonal.

steps.x: **E. Squamous cell carcinoma.** Squamous cell: cavitation, HPOA, PTHrP hypercalcaemia, keratin pearls.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with a 70 pack-year smoking history has a 5 week history of cough and breathlessness. Bronchoscopy shows an endobronchial tumour in the left main bronchus. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm and dense neurosecretory granules on electron microscopy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his chest X-ray?
questions.e: Neurosecretory granules mean small cell lung cancer, which arises from a main bronchus and appears as a central (perihilar) mass on chest X-ray.

steps.x: **Neurosecretory granules** = neuroendocrine origin = **small cell**. It arises from the bronchus, so it sits **centrally**.

elim: Pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure, not a bronchial tumour.
Reticular lower zone shadowing is pulmonary fibrosis.
Cavitation is squamous cell; peripheral lesions are adenocarcinoma.
A calcified granuloma is old healed tuberculosis.

steps.x: **C. Central hilar mass.** SCLC = central, perihilar, strongest smoking link.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man who stopped smoking 20 years ago has a 2 month history of a dry cough and new tender breast swelling. He takes no medicines. Chest X-ray shows a 3 cm mass at the periphery of the left lower lobe. CT-guided biopsy shows glandular spaces lined by tumour cells containing mucin.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A peripheral mass with mucin-containing glands is adenocarcinoma, which can also cause gynaecomastia; squamous cell shows keratin pearls instead.

clues: periphery of the left lower lobe
steps.x: **Glands with mucin** = adenocarcinoma (from mucus-secreting glandular cells). It is **peripheral** and can cause **gynaecomastia**.

elim: Carcinoid is a neuroendocrine tumour with granules, not mucin-filled glands.
Large cell is poorly differentiated with no glands or mucin.
SCLC is central with small blue cells and neurosecretory granules.
Squamous cell shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges and is central.

steps.x: **A. Adenocarcinoma of the lung.** Adenocarcinoma: most common subtype, peripheral, smokers and non-smokers, mucin on histology.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has a 2 month history of cough and 7 kg weight loss. He has smoked for 50 years. CT shows a 6 cm peripheral mass in the right upper lobe. Biopsy shows sheets of large undifferentiated cells with no gland formation, keratin or neuroendocrine features. His calcium and sodium are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Large cell carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion: poorly differentiated cells without glandular, squamous or neuroendocrine features, linked to smoking, with a poor prognosis.

clues: no gland formation, keratin or neuroendocrine features
steps.x: No glands (not adeno), no keratin (not squamous), no neuroendocrine features (not small cell) = **large cell**, poorly differentiated.

elim: Adenocarcinoma forms glands containing mucin.
Mesothelioma arises from the pleura and presents with effusion and thickening.
SCLC shows neuroendocrine granules and is central.
Squamous cell shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

steps.x: **B. Large cell carcinoma.** Large cell: undifferentiated, smoking-linked, no paraneoplastic syndrome, poor prognosis.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has a 6 week history of a new cough, two episodes of coughing up blood-streaked sputum and breathlessness on hills. He has lost 6 kg and has night sweats. He has a 45 pack-year smoking history and has not travelled abroad. He has no TB contacts. His temperature is 36.9°C and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A new persistent cough with haemoptysis and weight loss in a heavy smoker is lung cancer until proven otherwise; TB is less likely without travel, contacts or fever.

steps.x: A **new persistent cough** in a smoker plus **haemoptysis** (red flag) and **weight loss** = lung cancer.

elim: Bronchiectasis gives years of daily purulent sputum, not a new cough with weight loss.
PE is sudden, with pleuritic pain, not 6 weeks of weight loss and night sweats.
TB is possible with night sweats, but he has no travel, contacts or fever.
Sarcoidosis affects younger adults and rarely causes haemoptysis or weight loss.

steps.x: **B. Lung cancer.** New persistent cough in a smoker = lung cancer until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed 2 months ago has a 10 day history of headaches that are worst on waking, with vomiting. Her husband says she has become clumsy with her right hand. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 64 bpm and BP 152/88 mmHg. She has bilateral papilloedema. Her sodium and calcium are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema and a focal deficit mean raised intracranial pressure from a mass; the brain is the most common site of lung cancer metastasis.

steps.x: Raised ICP pattern (**morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema**) + **focal sign** in a cancer patient = brain metastasis.

elim: She has no fever or neck stiffness, and meningitis is acute.
Her calcium is normal and hypercalcaemia does not cause focal signs.
IIH affects young obese women and has no focal weakness.
Her sodium is normal and SIADH causes confusion, not focal signs and papilloedema.

steps.x: **B. Brain metastases.** The brain is the most common site of lung cancer metastasis.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 4 month history of dull left chest pain, breathlessness and 6 kg weight loss. She has never smoked. For 30 years she washed the work overalls of her husband, who fitted insulation in power stations. Her oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. There is dullness to percussion at the left base.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Left pleural effusion with irregular pleural thickening.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms
questions.e: Secondary asbestos exposure from washing overalls with chest pain and weight loss suggests mesothelioma, which shows a pleural effusion with pleural thickening.

clues: dullness to percussion at the left base
steps.x: Washing overalls of an insulation worker = **asbestos** exposure. Dull chest pain + weight loss = **mesothelioma**.

elim: Bilateral hilar nodes suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma.
A cavitating central mass is squamous cell carcinoma in a smoker.
Consolidation is pneumonia, with fever and productive cough.
Upper lobe fibrosis follows TB, sarcoid or ankylosing spondylitis.

steps.x: **D. Pleural effusion with pleural thickening.** Mesothelioma: asbestos, chest pain, effusion and pleural thickening on CXR.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with a 50 pack-year smoking history has a 2 month history of difficulty getting up from chairs and a dry mouth. Her hip flexors are weak, but power improves after repeated effort. Reflexes are reduced and return after exercise. Chest X-ray shows a left hilar mass.
questions.q: Which antibody is most likely to be found?
questions.e: Proximal leg weakness that improves with exertion, reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms with a hilar mass is Lambert-Eaton syndrome from SCLC, caused by anti-VGCC antibodies.

steps.x: Weakness that **improves with exertion** = Lambert-Eaton (myasthenia **worsens**). Hilar mass in a smoker = SCLC.

elim: These cause myasthenia gravis, which worsens with repeated effort.
Anti-Hu causes sensory neuropathy and encephalitis, not weakness that improves with effort.
Anti-MuSK is a form of myasthenia with fatigable bulbar weakness.
Anti-Yo causes cerebellar degeneration with gynaecological or breast cancers.

steps.x: **D. Anti-voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies.** LEMS = anti-VGCC antibodies, a paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung cancer.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 3 month history of aching in his right shoulder and inner arm. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. His face does not sweat on the right on a hot day. Chest X-ray shows a right apical opacity.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his eyes?
o: Dilated right pupil with complete ptosis
Small right pupil with partial ptosis
questions.e: A right apical (Pancoast) tumour compresses the cervical sympathetic chain, causing Horner's syndrome: miosis, partial ptosis and anhidrosis on the same side.

clues: does not sweat on the right
steps.x: Apical mass + one-sided **anhidrosis** = **Pancoast tumour** with **Horner's syndrome**.

elim: Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral and due to neurosyphilis.
This is a third nerve palsy, not sympathetic loss.
Proptosis and lid retraction are thyroid eye disease.
A RAPD is an optic nerve lesion.

steps.x: **E. Small right pupil with partial ptosis.** Horner's = miosis, partial ptosis, anhidrosis, same side as the apical tumour.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with a 55 pack-year smoking history has a 2 week history of a full feeling in his head and swelling around his eyes on waking. His face is red and his neck veins are distended and do not pulsate. When he raises both arms above his head for a minute his face darkens and he develops stridor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Facial plethora, periorbital oedema, distended non-pulsatile neck veins and a positive Pemberton's test in a smoker are superior vena cava obstruction from lung cancer.

clues: raises both arms above his head
steps.x: **Non-pulsatile** distended neck veins + facial plethora + positive **Pemberton's test** = SVC obstruction.

elim: Anaphylaxis is sudden with urticaria and hypotension, not 2 weeks of facial fullness.
Angioedema does not distend the neck veins or worsen on raising the arms.
Tamponade gives hypotension and a raised JVP that rises on inspiration, not facial plethora.
Right heart failure gives a pulsatile raised JVP with leg oedema, not facial swelling.

steps.x: **E. Superior vena cava obstruction.** SVCO is an oncological emergency; the commonest cause is lung cancer.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with small cell lung cancer has 1 week of nausea, headache and confusion. He is not on diuretics. He is clinically euvolaemic with no oedema. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hyponatraemia?
questions.e: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality but inappropriately concentrated urine high in sodium is SIADH, from ectopic ADH secretion by small cell lung cancer.

steps.x: Low serum osmolality + **concentrated urine** + euvolaemia = **SIADH**, the classic SCLC paraneoplastic syndrome.

elim: Addison's gives hypotension, hyperkalaemia and hypovolaemia.
Hypothyroidism rarely causes sodium this low and his TSH is normal.
Polydipsia gives a dilute urine, not a urine osmolality of 540.
He takes no diuretics.

steps.x: **D. Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion.** SCLC secretes ADH: think SIADH in any SCLC patient who becomes confused.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 month history of cough and weight loss. He has never smoked. At 24 years of age he had chest radiotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. He works as an accountant. CT chest shows a 3 cm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe.
questions.q: Which is the most likely risk factor for his lung tumour?
questions.e: Radiotherapy is a recognised risk factor for lung cancer, alongside smoking, asbestos and beryllium; in a never-smoker, prior chest radiotherapy is the clear cause here.

steps.x: Never smoked, so look for the other risks: **radiotherapy**, asbestos, beryllium.

elim: Asthma is not a risk factor for lung cancer.
Accountancy carries no carcinogen exposure.
Birds cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not lung cancer.
Previous pneumonia does not cause lung cancer.

steps.x: **D. Previous chest radiotherapy.** Lung cancer risks: smoking (most important), asbestos, beryllium, radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman has a 5 week history of cough and tiredness. She has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 45 years. She has lost 4 kg and wakes with night sweats. Her oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air and her chest is clear. Her GP arranges a full blood count before her chest X-ray.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her full blood count?
questions.e: Raised platelets are a feature of lung cancer and, in a smoker over 40 with cough and weight loss, are a trigger for an urgent chest X-ray.

clues: smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 45 years
steps.x: Smoker with cough, weight loss and night sweats = suspected lung cancer, which gives **raised platelets**.

elim: Eosinophilia suggests asthma, parasites or drug reactions.
Lymphocytosis suggests viral infection or CLL.
Neutropenia follows chemotherapy, not the presentation of cancer.
Lung cancer raises, rather than lowers, the platelet count.

steps.x: **E. Thrombocytosis.** Thrombocytosis is a lung cancer feature that should prompt an urgent chest X-ray.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman sees her GP after coughing up a teaspoon of fresh blood on two occasions this week. She has smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years. She has no fever, chest pain or leg swelling. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Two-week wait referral for suspected lung cancer
questions.e: Unexplained haemoptysis in anyone over 40 meets NICE criteria for a two-week wait urgent referral for suspected lung cancer.

clues: coughing up a teaspoon of fresh blood
no fever, chest pain or leg swelling
steps.x: Age **over 40** + **unexplained haemoptysis** = two-week wait referral.

elim: She has no signs of infection to explain the haemoptysis.
Watchful waiting delays diagnosis of a red-flag symptom.
A routine referral is too slow for unexplained haemoptysis.
Sputum culture does not exclude cancer and delays referral.

steps.x: **E. Two-week wait referral for suspected lung cancer.** Two-week wait: over 40 with unexplained haemoptysis, or a CXR suggesting lung cancer.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 2 month history of cough and weight loss. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history. Chest X-ray (see item resources) shows a 4 cm mass in the right upper zone. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. He has been referred under the two-week wait pathway.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Round 4 cm mass in the right upper zone.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: After an abnormal chest X-ray, contrast-enhanced CT chest is the second-line test to stage the disease and guide biopsy; bronchoscopy follows it.

clues: 4 cm mass in the right upper zone
steps.x: CXR shows the mass, then **contrast CT** stages it and plans the biopsy.

elim: Bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis but is planned after the contrast CT.
MRI is not used to stage lung cancer.
Sputum cytology is insensitive and does not stage.
V/Q scanning is for pulmonary embolism.

steps.x: **A. Contrast-enhanced CT chest.** Order: CXR, then contrast CT chest, then bronchoscopy or CT-guided biopsy.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has a 2.5 cm spiculated nodule at the outer edge of the left lower lobe on contrast CT, 1 cm from the pleura. There is no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. She is an ex-smoker. Her oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air and her clotting screen is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: A peripheral lesion out of bronchoscopic reach is confirmed by CT-guided biopsy; central lesions are reached by fibre-optic bronchoscopy.

clues: outer edge of the left lower lobe
steps.x: **Peripheral** lesion (typical of adenocarcinoma) = out of the bronchoscope's reach, so take tissue under **CT guidance**.

elim: A 2.5 cm spiculated lesion needs tissue now, not surveillance.
PET stages disease but does not give a tissue diagnosis.
Tumour markers do not confirm lung cancer.
Sputum cytology is insensitive, especially for peripheral tumours.

steps.x: **A. CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy.** Central lesion: bronchoscopy. Peripheral lesion: CT-guided biopsy.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has a 3 cm squamous cell carcinoma in the left lower lobe confirmed on bronchoscopic biopsy. Contrast CT chest and upper abdomen shows no enlarged lymph nodes and no liver or adrenal lesions. He is fit and keen to have surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before planning surgery?
questions.e: Before curative surgery, PET-CT is used to look for occult nodal or distant spread missed on CT.

steps.x: Diagnosis made, CT looks clear, surgery planned: **PET-CT** checks for hidden spread first.

elim: A bone scan only looks at bone; PET-CT surveys the whole body.
Delaying staging lets a curable tumour progress.
The diagnosis is already confirmed by biopsy.
CT has already imaged the abdomen better than ultrasound.

steps.x: **B. PET-CT.** PET-CT is the staging test before radical treatment.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has a 2.5 cm adenocarcinoma confined to the right upper lobe with no nodal or distant spread on PET-CT. He has a 40 pack-year history and gets breathless after two flights of stairs. The thoracic surgeons are considering a lobectomy.
questions.q: Which investigation is essential before surgery?
questions.e: Lobectomy needs pulmonary function tests first; an FEV1 below 1.5 L contraindicates it.

clues: confined to the right upper lobe
breathless after two flights of stairs
steps.x: Surgery removes lung, so prove there is enough lung reserve first: **spirometry/PFTs**.

elim: A blood gas does not show whether he can tolerate losing a lobe.
The diagnosis and stage are already established.
There is no cardiac history to need an echo first.
This tests for ischaemia, not lung reserve.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary function tests.** Before lobectomy: pulmonary function tests (FEV1 <1.5 L is a contraindication).

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a CT chest for persistent cough. It shows a single 7 mm solid nodule in the right middle lobe with smooth margins. There is no lymphadenopathy. He stopped smoking 10 years ago. His cough has since settled.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Nodules in the 5 to 8 mm range are kept under surveillance with a repeat CT at 12 months.

steps.x: Size is everything: **7 mm** sits in the 5 to 8 mm surveillance band.

elim: A 7 mm nodule is too small to biopsy and is in the surveillance range.
Nodules of 5 to 8 mm need surveillance.
PET is unreliable in nodules under 8 mm.
A 7 mm nodule is often invisible on chest X-ray.

steps.x: **E. Repeat CT chest at 12 months.** 5 to 8 mm nodule = repeat CT at 12 months.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man sees his GP with a cough that has lasted 4 weeks. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day since he was 16. He has no haemoptysis or weight loss. His temperature is 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His chest is clear. The GP requests a chest X-ray.
questions.q: Within which time frame should the chest X-ray be performed?
questions.e: A smoker over 40 with an unexplained cough lasting over 3 weeks needs a chest X-ray within 2 weeks to look for lung cancer.

steps.x: Smoker over 40 + **persistent cough** = first-line **CXR within 2 weeks**.

elim: A persistent cough in a smoker already justifies a CXR.
He is well; same-day imaging is for emergencies.
Three months is too long to wait for possible cancer.
Six weeks is the old routine wait, too slow here.

steps.x: **B. Within 2 weeks.** First-line test for suspected lung cancer: chest X-ray within 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman who has never smoked has stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lung with bone metastases. She works full time and walks her dog daily. Molecular testing of the biopsy shows an activating EGFR mutation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Advanced NSCLC with an actionable mutation such as EGFR is treated with targeted therapy chosen by tumour markers.

steps.x: Stage IV = not for surgery. A **driver mutation** = **targeted** therapy.

elim: She is fit, so active treatment is appropriate.
Surgery is not curative once the cancer has spread to bone.
Surgery is not used for stage IV disease.
Radiotherapy to the chest does not treat her bone metastases.

steps.x: **B. EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor.** Advanced NSCLC: test for tumour markers; use targeted or immunotherapy where they apply.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has stage IIIB squamous cell carcinoma of the right lung with mediastinal nodal spread. He is independent and active. Molecular testing shows no targetable mutation. His renal function and hearing are normal. FEV1 is 2.1 L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Stage III/IV NSCLC without a targetable mutation is treated with platinum-based chemotherapy, for example cisplatin plus gemcitabine.

steps.x: Stage III/IV NSCLC with **no driver mutation** = **platinum chemotherapy** (normal kidneys and hearing allow cisplatin).

elim: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML and GIST, not lung cancer.
Advanced disease in a fit man needs active treatment.
Dexamethasone is for SVCO or brain metastases, not first-line treatment.
Nodal spread (stage III) is beyond curative lobectomy.

steps.x: **A. Cisplatin plus gemcitabine.** Stage III/IV NSCLC: cisplatin plus gemcitabine.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has a 3 cm adenocarcinoma in the left upper lobe with no nodal spread. He is being assessed for lobectomy. His voice is normal and his chest X-ray shows no effusion. His BP is 138/82 mmHg. Results of pre-operative tests are given.
questions.q: Which finding most contraindicates surgery?
questions.e: An FEV1 below 1.5 L means he lacks the lung reserve for a lobectomy; age alone is not a contraindication.

steps.x: Check each contraindication: SVCO, effusion, cord palsy are all absent. Only **FEV1 <1.5 L** remains.

elim: Age alone does not exclude lobectomy.
Smoking history does not by itself prevent surgery.
A normal voice argues against recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion.
One-lobe disease is the indication for lobectomy.

steps.x: **C. FEV1 1.2 L.** Surgery is contraindicated by SVCO, FEV1 <1.5 L, malignant effusion or vocal cord paralysis.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with mesothelioma has a right pleural effusion that has been aspirated twice in 3 weeks. Each time he became breathless again within days. He is breathless walking to the bathroom and wants to spend his remaining time at home. His oxygen saturation is 91% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his effusion?
questions.e: A recurrent symptomatic malignant pleural effusion is best managed with an indwelling pleural catheter, which he can drain at home.

steps.x: **Recurrent** malignant effusion + wants to be **at home** = indwelling pleural catheter.

elim: A malignant exudate does not respond to diuretics.
Major surgery is not appropriate for symptom control in advanced disease.
It re-accumulates within days, so repeated aspiration fails.
Radiotherapy does not drain a recurrent effusion.

steps.x: **C. Indwelling pleural catheter.** Symptomatic malignant pleural effusion: indwelling pleural catheter.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with small cell lung cancer has facial swelling and distended non-pulsatile neck veins. She was given oral dexamethasone 8 mg in the Emergency Department yesterday. Her breathing is comfortable. CT venogram confirms tumour compressing the superior vena cava.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management of the obstruction?
questions.e: SVC obstruction is treated with oral dexamethasone 8 mg immediately and then definitively with an SVC stent.

clues: tumour compressing the superior vena cava
steps.x: Dexamethasone has been given; the **definitive** step reopens the vein: **SVC stent**.

elim: Diuretics do not relieve mechanical compression of the SVC.
SVC obstruction is a contraindication to lung cancer surgery.
This is tumour compression, not a thrombus.
Anticoagulation does not relieve tumour compression.

steps.x: **A. Endovascular SVC stent.** SVCO: dexamethasone 8 mg now, then SVC stent.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has metastatic non-small cell lung cancer in his liver and bones. He has had two lines of chemotherapy and his disease has progressed. He now spends most of the day in bed, is breathless and in pain, and says he does not want further treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: In advanced, incurable lung cancer with poor performance status, specialist palliative care for symptom control is the priority.

clues: spends most of the day in bed
steps.x: Progressed, bed-bound, **declines treatment** = focus on **symptom control**.

elim: He has progressed on chemotherapy, is bed-bound and declines treatment.
Surgery has no role in metastatic disease.
Further staging will not change care he has declined.
He has no brain metastases.

steps.x: **C. Referral to specialist palliative care.** Advanced or refractory lung cancer: palliative care is central.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung has 1 week of thirst, constipation and drowsiness. His pulse rate is 112 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and his mucous membranes are dry. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in management?
questions.e: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia with dehydration is treated first with IV 0.9% sodium chloride; a bisphosphonate comes only after rehydration.

steps.x: Squamous cell + high calcium with low PTH = **PTHrP**. He is dry and hypotensive, so **fluids first**.

elim: Furosemide in a dehydrated patient worsens hypovolaemia.
A bisphosphonate may follow, but rehydration comes first.
Steroids are for SVCO or cord compression, not PTHrP hypercalcaemia.
Calcitonin is a weak, short-lived second-line agent.

steps.x: **A. IV 0.9% sodium chloride.** Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: IV 0.9% sodium chloride first.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has a central squamous cell carcinoma. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He asks why smoking caused his cancer when he never had a chest infection. Biopsy shows malignant cells arising from the bronchial lining.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which smoking caused his tumour?
o: Carcinogen-induced mutations in bronchial epithelial cells
Immune complex deposition in the lung
Repeated bacterial infection of the bronchi
questions.e: Carcinogens in tobacco smoke cause accumulated genetic mutations in bronchial epithelial cells, leading to malignant transformation.

clues: smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 40 years
steps.x: Cancer = **accumulated DNA mutations**; tobacco carcinogens act on the **bronchial epithelium**.

elim: Protease-antiprotease imbalance causes emphysema, not cancer.
Eosinophilic inflammation is asthma.
Immune complexes cause vasculitis and hypersensitivity, not carcinoma.
Infection does not drive malignant transformation.

steps.x: **B. Carcinogen-induced mutations in bronchial epithelial cells.** Lung cancer: carcinogens (tobacco, asbestos, radon) cause mutations in bronchial epithelium.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman has a small cell lung cancer in the right main bronchus. At diagnosis CT shows liver and adrenal deposits. She asks why surgery is not being offered, as her friend had a lung tumour removed. She is offered combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
questions.q: Which feature of small cell lung cancer best explains why surgery is not used?
o: Peripheral location out of surgical reach
Slow growth with little benefit from removal
questions.e: Small cell lung cancer arises from neuroendocrine cells and behaves aggressively, usually having metastasised by diagnosis, so it is treated with chemoradiotherapy.

steps.x: Spread already present **at diagnosis** = surgery cannot clear it. SCLC is **aggressive** and metastasises early.

elim: That is adenocarcinoma; SCLC is neuroendocrine.
SCLC is central, not peripheral.
SCLC is initially very chemosensitive.
SCLC is aggressive and fast-growing.

steps.x: **A. Early widespread metastasis.** SCLC: neuroendocrine, aggressive, early spread, so chemoradiotherapy rather than surgery.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with a 55 pack-year history has 2 months of cough and weight loss. He has no fever and sputum is not purulent. Chest X-ray (see item resources) shows a thick-walled cavity near the left hilum. Biopsy shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Thick-walled cavity near the left hilum.

questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the cavity?
o: Necrosis in the centre of the tumour
questions.e: Squamous cell carcinoma arises centrally near the bronchi and outgrows its blood supply, so its centre necroses and cavitates.

clues: thick-walled cavity near the left hilum
steps.x: **Keratin pearls** = squamous cell. Central tumours outgrow their blood supply and **necrose centrally**.

elim: He has no fever or purulent sputum, and histology shows tumour.
Histology shows squamous carcinoma, not granulomas.
A bulla is thin-walled and not lined by keratinising tumour.
Septic emboli give multiple peripheral cavities with fever.

steps.x: **C. Necrosis in the centre of the tumour.** Squamous cell cavitates from central necrosis.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with a right hilar lung mass has 10 days of swelling of her face, neck and both arms, worse when she bends forward. Her ankles are not swollen. Dilated veins are visible over her upper chest wall. Her BP is 136/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her swelling?
o: Impaired venous return from tumour compressing the SVC
questions.e: A hilar tumour compresses or invades the superior vena cava, impairing venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs, so only the upper body swells and collateral chest veins dilate.

clues: Dilated veins are visible over her upper chest wall
steps.x: Swelling confined to the area drained by the **SVC**, sparing the legs, with **collateral veins** = SVC compression.

elim: Low albumin causes generalised and dependent oedema, including the ankles.
Axillary lymphatic block causes one-arm lymphoedema, not facial swelling.
Raised right heart pressure causes leg oedema and ascites too.
Allergy gives sudden swelling with urticaria, not 10 days of venous distension.

steps.x: **B. Impaired venous return from tumour compressing the SVC.** SVCO: tumour compresses the SVC, blocking return from head, neck and arms.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung has an adjusted calcium of 3.21 mmol/L. He has no bone metastases on bone scan. His vitamin D level is normal. A parathyroid hormone level and serum phosphate are requested.
questions.q: Which pattern of results is most likely?
questions.e: PTHrP mimics PTH on bone and kidney, raising calcium and causing phosphate loss in the urine, while the high calcium suppresses native PTH.

steps.x: No bone metastases + squamous cell = **PTHrP**. It acts like PTH on the kidney (**phosphate falls**) but native **PTH is suppressed**.

elim: This pattern fits secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal failure.
This is primary hyperparathyroidism, where PTH itself is raised.
Low PTH with high phosphate fits vitamin D excess or bone destruction.
High calcium should suppress PTH, and PTHrP lowers phosphate.

steps.x: **D. PTH low, phosphate low.** PTHrP: high calcium, low phosphate, suppressed PTH.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has a 4 month history of burning pain down the inner side of her left arm into her little finger. She has wasting of the small muscles of the left hand. She has a 35 pack-year smoking history. CT shows a mass at the left lung apex invading the chest wall.
questions.q: Which structure has the tumour most likely invaded to cause her hand signs?
o: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus
Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
questions.e: An apical (Pancoast) tumour directly invades the lower brachial plexus (C8 to T1), causing pain on the inner arm and wasting of the small hand muscles.

clues: inner side of her left arm into her little finger
steps.x: Inner arm + little finger + small hand muscles = **C8/T1**, which lie right above the lung apex.

elim: Carpal tunnel affects the thumb side and spares the little finger.
Phrenic nerve palsy paralyses the diaphragm, not the hand.
This causes hoarseness, not hand wasting.
This lesion would not be caused by an apical lung tumour and spares the inner arm.

steps.x: **A. Lower trunk of the brachial plexus.** Pancoast tumour invades the sympathetic chain, brachial plexus and recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with a central lung mass has hyponatraemia from SIADH. Six weeks later he develops proximal leg weakness that improves with exercise. A medical student asks why this tumour type, and not the others, so often produces hormones and autoantibody syndromes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: It arises from mucus-secreting glandular cells
It metastasises to the adrenal glands
questions.e: Small cell lung cancer arises from neuroendocrine cells, so it can ectopically secrete hormones (ADH, ACTH) and trigger autoantibodies such as anti-VGCC in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

steps.x: SIADH + Lambert-Eaton = **small cell**. Its **neuroendocrine** origin explains hormone secretion.

elim: That is the origin of adenocarcinoma, which has no paraneoplastic link.
Ectopic hormones come from the tumour itself, not pituitary invasion.
Adrenal deposits do not cause SIADH or Lambert-Eaton.
Keratin is a feature of squamous cell, which secretes PTHrP instead.

steps.x: **B. It arises from neuroendocrine cells.** SCLC: neuroendocrine cells, ectopic ADH/ACTH, anti-VGCC antibodies.
